Use the "Validate fix" button in Search Console to track. ### Common mistakes - Chasing a Lighthouse score of 100 while field data is fine (or vice versa). - Lazy-loading everything including the hero image. - Ignoring third-party scripts because "marketing needs them" — audit their value.
keyTakeaways: Good thresholds at the 75th percentile: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1; INP replaced FID in March 2024.
Judge success with field data (CrUX, Search Console, RUM); use lab tools to debug.
LCP: fix TTFB, discovery, weight and render delay; INP: break long tasks; CLS: reserve space.
CWV are a ranking input but not a shortcut to top positions; prioritise by template and business value.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which metric replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: INP became a Core Web Vital in March 2024, replacing FID.

knowledgeCheck.question: The LCP element is a hero image with loading="lazy" set by a theme. Best fix?
options: Convert it to a CSS background
Remove lazy-loading from the hero and give it high fetch priority
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Lazy-loading delays the LCP resource. The LCP image should load eagerly with fetchpriority=high; CSS backgrounds are discovered later.

knowledgeCheck.question: Lighthouse shows a perfect score but Search Console shows poor INP on mobile. Which should you trust for user experience?
options: Search Console field data, because it reflects real users
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Field data reflects real users and devices; lab tools cannot fully measure INP.

lessons.activity: Run PageSpeed Insights on your three highest-traffic templates, record field LCP/INP/CLS, and identify the dominant cause for the worst metric on each.

lessons.title: Mobile-first indexing, HTTPS and security headers
lessons.body:
### Mobile-first indexing in practice

Google predominantly uses the **mobile version** of content, crawled with the smartphone Googlebot, for indexing and ranking. For responsive sites where the same HTML serves every device, this is mostly a non-issue. Problems appear when the mobile experience differs from desktop.

### The parity checklist

Your mobile version should have the same:

- **Primary content** — text, images, videos. Content hidden in accordions or tabs for mobile UX is fine as long as it is in the HTML; content *removed* from mobile is effectively removed from Google.
- **Meta data** — titles, meta descriptions, robots meta. A mobile template that accidentally outputs `noindex` affects the whole index.
- **Structured data** — same markup, pointing to mobile URLs on separate-URL setups.
- **Internal links** — a slimmed-down mobile menu that drops links to key categories reduces discovery and internal link signals.
- **Images** — same quality, supported formats, descriptive alt text; lazy-loading that works without user interaction.
- **Lazy-loaded content** — loaded based on visibility in the viewport, not on swipe or click.

For legacy separate mobile sites (`m.example.com`), you need `rel="alternate"` from desktop to mobile and `rel="canonical"` from mobile to desktop, plus equivalent content. Migrating to responsive design removes a whole class of errors and is recommended.

How to check: use URL Inspection (which uses the smartphone crawler), crawl with a mobile user agent, and compare content, links and directives against a desktop crawl.

### Intrusive interstitials

Full-screen pop-ups that block content right after a user arrives from search create a poor experience. Legally required interstitials (cookie consent, age verification) are acceptable; design them to be small and dismissible. Keep the underlying content in the HTML so it can still be crawled.

### HTTPS

HTTPS is a lightweight ranking signal and a baseline of trust. Checklist:

1. Valid certificate covering all hosts (www and non-www, subdomains).
2. Sitewide 301 from HTTP to HTTPS in a single hop.
3. Canonicals, hreflang, sitemaps and internal links all use `https://` URLs.
4. No **mixed content** (HTTP images, scripts or iframes on HTTPS pages); browsers block or warn.
5. Modern TLS configuration (TLS 1.2 minimum, TLS 1.3 preferred).

### Security headers

Security headers are not ranking factors in their own right, but they protect users and your site's reputation, and a hacked site suffers severely in search (spam injections, malware warnings, manual actions). A sensible baseline:

```text
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com data:; script-src 'self' https://www.googletagmanager.com; frame-ancestors 'self'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()
```

Notes:

- **HSTS** forces HTTPS for returning browsers. Start with a short `max-age`, confirm every subdomain supports HTTPS, then increase. Only add `preload` when you are certain — preload lists are slow to undo.
- **CSP** prevents many script injection attacks; deploy first as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` to discover what would break (tag managers and third-party widgets often need allow-listing).
- `frame-ancestors` in CSP supersedes the older `X-Frame-Options` for clickjacking protection.
- Set a `Referrer-Policy` that keeps origin data for analytics while not leaking full URLs cross-site.

### Hacked-site and spam monitoring

- Watch Search Console's **Security issues** and **Manual actions** reports; enable email notifications.
- Use `site:example.com` searches with spam terms (pharma, casino, replica) occasionally to spot injected pages; also check for unfamiliar URLs in the Page indexing report and Performance queries in languages you do not publish in.
- Keep CMS, themes and plugins patched; remove unused plugins; enforce multi-factor authentication for admin accounts.
- If compromised: clean, close the vulnerability, then request a review in Search Console.

### Common mistakes

- A mobile template with fewer internal links or missing structured data.
- Mixed content after a CDN or image domain change.
- Setting HSTS with `includeSubDomains` before a legacy subdomain supports HTTPS — it becomes unreachable for returning visitors.
- Believing security headers themselves will lift rankings; their value is protection.
keyTakeaways: Google indexes the mobile version; content, links, meta and structured data must match desktop.
Content hidden in tabs is fine if it is in the HTML; content removed on mobile is lost to Google.
HTTPS needs single-hop redirects, HTTPS URLs everywhere and no mixed content.
Security headers protect users and reputation rather than directly boosting rankings; roll out HSTS and CSP carefully.

knowledgeCheck.question: A responsive redesign hides the FAQ section on mobile using CSS display:none but keeps it in the HTML. Impact on mobile-first indexing?
options: The content is still in the HTML so it can be indexed
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Content in the HTML but visually collapsed or hidden for UX is still available to Google. Content removed from the mobile HTML is not.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the safest way to introduce a Content Security Policy?
options: Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and review reports
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Report-only mode shows what would break without blocking anything, so you can refine the policy.

lessons.activity: Compare mobile and desktop crawls of your site for word count, internal link count, structured data and robots directives on five templates; list any parity gaps.

modules.title: Migrations, auditing workflow and monitoring
modules.summary: Run site migrations without losing visibility, audit systematically, and monitor with Search Console so problems are caught in days, not months.

lessons.title: Site migrations: a zero-drama checklist
lessons.body:
### What counts as a migration

Any change that alters URLs, hosts, templates or rendering at scale: **domain change**, **HTTP to HTTPS**, **URL restructure**, **platform/CMS change** (e.g. WordPress to Shopify, or a move to a headless front end), **merging sites**, and **major redesigns**. Several at once multiplies risk — if you can, separate a domain move from a replatform.

Even perfect migrations can cause temporary fluctuation while Google recrawls and reprocesses. Google has said a medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move, and larger sites longer. Set expectations in writing before you start.

### Phase 1: Planning (weeks before)

1. **Define scope and owners.** Who signs off redirects, who deploys, who monitors?
2. **Benchmark everything:** full crawl of the old site; Search Console exports (performance by page and query, Page indexing counts); analytics landing-page traffic and conversions; rank tracking for priority queries; backlink list of top-linked URLs; log sample.
3. **Inventory URLs** from all sources: crawl, sitemaps, Search Console, analytics, backlinks, logs. Crawls alone miss old URLs that still receive links.
4. **Build the redirect map** — old URL to most relevant new URL, one hop, 301/308. Prioritise by traffic, links and revenue. Pages with no equivalent get 404/410 intentionally.

```text
old_url,new_url,type,priority,notes
/services/seo-audit.html,/services/technical-seo-audit/,301,high,top converter
/blog/2019/05/gbp-tips,/guides/google-business-profile/,301,high,merged into guide
/careers/intern-2018,,410,low,no equivalent
```

5. **Plan content and template parity.** Titles, meta descriptions, headings, body content, internal links, structured data, hreflang, canonicals, image alt text — carry them over or consciously improve them.
6. **Choose timing** away from peak seasons (Ramadan and Eid campaigns for Gulf retailers, Black Friday, Diwali, back-to-school).

### Phase 2: Staging and pre-launch QA

- Staging protected by authentication (not only robots.txt).
- Crawl staging and compare against the benchmark: missing pages, title changes, lost internal links, structured data errors, canonicals pointing at staging hosts.
- **Test the redirect map** against staging with a list crawl: every old URL should return one 301 to a 200 destination.
- Check robots.txt and meta robots for the **production** configuration — confirm `Disallow: /` and staging `noindex` will not ship.
- Check rendering and Core Web Vitals of new templates.
- Prepare new XML sitemaps.

### Phase 3: Launch day

1. Deploy redirects together with the new site.
2. Verify robots.txt, a sample of meta robots and canonicals on production immediately.
3. Crawl the old URL list: confirm 301s resolve in one hop to 200 pages.
4. **Domain moves:** verify both properties in Search Console and use the **Change of Address** tool (for domain-level moves).
5. Submit new sitemaps. Keeping a sitemap of old URLs available for a short time can help Google discover the redirects.
6. Update external profiles you control: Google Business Profile website link, social profiles, directories, ad destination URLs, email templates.

### Phase 4: Post-launch monitoring (first 4–12 weeks)

| Check | Frequency | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 404s and 5xx on old and new URLs | Daily, first two weeks | Logs, crawler, Search Console |
| Googlebot crawl of new URLs | Daily | Logs, Crawl stats |
| Indexing of new URLs vs old | Weekly | Page indexing, URL Inspection samples |
| Traffic and conversions by page group | Daily then weekly | Analytics vs benchmark |
| Rankings for priority queries | Weekly | Rank tracker |
| Structured data and CWV | Weekly | Enhancement and CWV reports |

Keep redirects in place for **at least a year** (Google's guidance), and ideally indefinitely. Keep the old domain registered.

### Worked example: platform change

A Lahore-based retailer moves from a custom PHP store to a hosted e-commerce platform. The platform forces `/products/` and `/collections/` URL patterns. The team exports every legacy URL (including those only found in backlinks and logs), maps products by SKU and categories by name, uses the platform's redirect manager for one-hop 301s, recreates custom title templates, and moves blog content with matching slugs where possible. After launch, logs reveal thousands of hits to old image URLs used in Google Images; they add image redirects too — a commonly forgotten item.

### Rollback criteria

Agree in advance what triggers a rollback or an emergency fix: for example, robots.txt blocking the site, redirects failing for a large share of legacy URLs, or checkout broken. Without predefined criteria, teams argue while visibility drops.

### Common mistakes

- Redirecting everything to the home page.
- Changing URLs, content and design at once without benchmarks, so nobody can diagnose drops.
- Removing redirects after a few months "because traffic moved".
- Forgetting image, PDF and hreflang URLs.
keyTakeaways: Benchmark crawl, Search Console, analytics, rankings and backlinks before any migration.
Build a one-hop 301 redirect map from every known old URL, prioritised by traffic, links and revenue.
QA staging and redirects before launch, and verify production robots.txt and directives immediately after.
Use Change of Address for domain moves, keep redirects at least a year, and monitor for weeks.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should you source old URLs for a migration redirect map?
options: Crawl, sitemaps, Search Console, analytics, backlink tools and server logs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Crawls miss URLs that are no longer linked internally but still receive links or traffic; combine sources.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which Search Console tool supports a domain name change?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Change of Address tool tells Google about a move from one domain to another, alongside 301 redirects.

knowledgeCheck.question: How long does Google recommend keeping migration redirects?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Google's site move guidance recommends keeping redirects for at least a year; many keep them indefinitely.

lessons.activity: Draft a migration plan outline for a site you know: benchmarks, URL sources, redirect map columns, QA steps, launch checks and rollback criteria.

lessons.title: Auditing workflow, tools and Search Console monitoring
lessons.body:
### A repeatable audit workflow

Senior technical SEOs work from a consistent sequence so nothing important is skipped and findings are comparable over time.

1. **Context** — business goals, priority templates, recent releases, known incidents, markets, CMS and hosting stack.
2. **Access** — Search Console (Domain property), Bing Webmaster Tools, analytics, logs or CDN logs, CMS read access, staging.
3. **Crawl** — a full crawl with JavaScript rendering where relevant, mobile user agent, and crawl-source integrations (sitemaps, Search Console, analytics).
4. **Indexation review** — Page indexing report by sitemap segment; sample URL Inspection.
5. **Template review** — for each key template: status, directives, canonical, rendering, content, internal links, structured data, CWV.
6. **Logs** — what bots actually crawl.
7. **Prioritise** — impact × effort × confidence, tied to business value.
8. **Report and ticket** — clear actions, owners, acceptance criteria.
9. **Verify and monitor** — recrawl, Search Console validation, alerting.

### The tool stack (vendor-neutral)

| Job | Examples |
|---|---|
| Desktop/cloud crawling | Screaming Frog SEO Spider, Sitebulb, Lumar, JetOctopus, Oncrawl |
| Google data | Search Console (UI, API, bulk data export to BigQuery) |
| Bing data | Bing Webmaster Tools (also useful because Bing's index feeds several AI assistants) |
| Performance | PageSpeed Insights, CrUX, Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools, RUM via web-vitals |
| Structured data | Rich Results Test, Schema Markup Validator |
| Logs | Log analysers from crawler vendors, BigQuery, ELK stack, CDN analytics |
| Change monitoring | Tools that alert on robots.txt, title, canonical or status changes; custom scripts |

The tool matters less than configuration. Always record crawl settings (user agent, rendering, limits, excluded patterns) in the audit so results are reproducible.

### Search Console: the reports that matter most

- **Page indexing** — why URLs are not indexed; filter by sitemap for segment-level views. Use "Validate fix" after resolving an issue type.
- **URL Inspection** — index status, Google-selected canonical, last crawl, crawl user agent, rendered HTML and resources (live test). The API supports bulk inspection within quota.
- **Performance** — clicks, impressions, CTR and position by query, page, country, device and search appearance. Use regex filters to segment brand vs non-brand.
- **Crawl stats** (Settings) — requests per day, response codes, file types, average response time, host status (robots.txt fetch, DNS, server connectivity).
- **Sitemaps** — submission status and discovered URLs.
- **Core Web Vitals** and **HTTPS** reports.
- **Enhancements** — structured data items by type.
- **Manual actions** and **Security issues** — check on every audit.
- **Removals** — temporary removals and outdated content requests.
- **robots.txt report** — fetched versions and errors per host.

### Monitoring: catch problems in days

Set up a lightweight monitoring layer:

1. **Email alerts** from Search Console (on by default for verified owners — make sure the right people are verified users).
2. **Scheduled crawls** of key templates weekly, compared to the previous run (new noindex, canonical changes, status changes, title changes).
3. **Change monitoring** on robots.txt and a set of critical URLs.
4. **Dashboards** — Search Console data by page group in a BI tool (Looker Studio, Power BI, or BigQuery with the bulk export), with annotations for releases.
5. **Log alerts** — spikes in 5xx to Googlebot, or drops in Googlebot hits.
6. **Release checklist** — SEO sign-off for changes affecting templates, routing or robots directives.

A simple regex to split brand and non-brand queries in the Performance report:

```text
^(?!.*(optimize ?all|optimiseall)).*$
```

### Reading Search Console data correctly

- Performance data is sampled and anonymised queries are omitted, so query totals will not sum to page totals.
- Average position is an impression-weighted average; mixing many queries hides detail. Analyse by query-page pairs.
- Report timelines lag by a few days; indexing reports update less frequently than performance data.
- Compare like-for-like periods (same weekday mix, seasonality such as Ramadan, Eid, Christmas or summer holidays).

### Common mistakes

- Running a crawler with default settings on a JavaScript site and reporting "no content".
- Delivering a 200-row spreadsheet with no priorities.
- Auditing once a year instead of monitoring continuously.
- Only verifying a URL-prefix property and missing subdomains or protocol variants (use a Domain property).

video.script: Most technical SEO disasters are not discovered by audits. They are discovered by traffic graphs, weeks too late. A noindex left on a template. A robots.txt copied from staging. A canonical that suddenly points to the home page. The fix is to treat technical SEO as monitoring, not a yearly event. Start with a repeatable audit workflow: understand the business and recent releases, get access to Search Console, logs and analytics, crawl with the right settings, review indexing, review each key template, check the logs, then prioritise by impact, effort and confidence. In Search Console, four reports do most of the work. Page indexing tells you why URLs are not indexed. Filter it by sitemap to see which section is struggling. URL Inspection shows the canonical Google picked and the HTML it rendered. Performance shows clicks and impressions by page, query and country. And Crawl stats, hidden under Settings, shows response codes and server response times for Googlebot. Then build a monitoring layer. Make sure the right people get Search Console emails. Schedule weekly crawls of key templates and compare them with the previous run. Watch robots.txt for changes. Alert on spikes of server errors to Googlebot. And add an SEO check to every release that touches templates or routing. Do this and you'll catch most problems in days, while they're still cheap to fix.

keyTakeaways: Use a consistent workflow: context, access, crawl, indexation, templates, logs, prioritise, ticket, verify.
Page indexing, URL Inspection, Performance and Crawl stats are the core Search Console reports for technical work.
Monitor continuously with alerts, scheduled crawls, change detection and release sign-off.
Interpret Search Console data carefully: sampling, anonymised queries and weighted average position.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which Search Console report shows average server response time for Googlebot and host status?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Crawl stats (under Settings) shows request volumes, response codes, response times and host status.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why use a Domain property rather than a URL-prefix property?
options: It includes all protocols and subdomains
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A Domain property aggregates http/https and all subdomains, avoiding blind spots.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why might the sum of query-level clicks be lower than page-level clicks?
options: Anonymised queries are omitted from query-level data
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Google omits rare, anonymised queries for privacy, so query tables do not sum to totals.

lessons.activity: Set up a weekly monitoring routine for a site: list the Search Console reports, crawl comparisons and alerts you will check, and who owns each.

pool.question: Which order correctly describes how a URL reaches search results?
pool.explanation: URLs are discovered (links, sitemaps), fetched, rendered, evaluated for indexing, then eligible to be served. Debugging follows the same order.

pool.question: URL Inspection's rendered HTML for a product page shows an empty product grid, while the page looks fine in your browser. What is the most likely cause?
options: The page has too many internal links
Resources needed to render (e.g. an API or JS bundle) are blocked or failing for Googlebot
The page title is too long
The XML sitemap is missing lastmod
pool.explanation: If rendering depends on blocked or failing resources, Google sees the empty shell. Titles, lastmod and link counts do not empty the rendered DOM.

pool.question: An SPA shows 'Product not found' for deleted products but returns HTTP 200. Which fixes are consistent with Google's guidance? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Add a robots meta noindex via JavaScript on the error view
Canonicalise the error view to the home page
Route unknown URLs to a server response with a 404 status
Add the URLs to the XML sitemap
pool.explanation: Google documents both a real 404 and JS-injected noindex for SPA error states. Sitemaps and home-page canonicals do not fix soft 404s.

pool.question: A site's raw HTML contains `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`, which JavaScript removes after load for indexable pages. What happens?
options: Google always renders and indexes the page
Google indexes the raw HTML only
Bing and Google both ignore the tag
Google may not render the page and will treat it as noindex
pool.explanation: Google may skip rendering when the initial HTML contains noindex, so the JavaScript removal is never processed.

pool.question: Which navigation link is reliably crawlable?
options: A URL only reachable via internal site search
pool.explanation: Google follows anchors with resolvable href values; click handlers and search-only paths are not reliable discovery routes.

pool.question: Why is hash-based routing (`/#/pricing`) a problem for SEO?
options: Google generally ignores the fragment, so all views look like one URL
pool.explanation: Fragments are typically ignored for indexing; use History API paths so each view has its own URL.

pool.question: Which directive keeps a crawlable HTML page out of Google's index?
pool.explanation: noindex is the indexing directive. Disallow blocks crawling; nofollow and sitemap priority do not remove pages.

pool.question: A team disallowed /old-offers/ in robots.txt and added noindex to those pages last month. They are still indexed. What should they do?
options: Wait; it always takes a year
Remove the Disallow so Google can crawl and see the noindex
Add the pages to the sitemap with priority 0
pool.explanation: Blocked pages cannot be crawled, so the noindex is never seen. Allow crawling until they drop out.

pool.question: Which of these does Googlebot ignore in robots.txt?
pool.explanation: Google does not support crawl-delay (Bing does). Disallow, Allow and Sitemap lines are supported.

pool.question: Rules for Googlebot: `Disallow: /shop/` and `Allow: /shop/sale/`. Which URLs can Googlebot crawl? (Choose all that apply.)
pool.explanation: The longer, more specific Allow wins for /shop/sale/…; /blog/shop-guide does not start with /shop/. /shop/shoes and /shop/ match the Disallow.

pool.question: Log analysis shows a large share of Googlebot requests hitting `?sort=` and `?view=` URLs while new products are crawled slowly. Best first action?
options: Stop linking to those parameter URLs internally and disallow the patterns in robots.txt
Submit each product in URL Inspection
pool.explanation: Removing crawl paths and disallowing useless parameters frees crawling for valuable URLs. noindex still requires crawling.

pool.question: You see heavy traffic with a Googlebot user agent from IPs that reverse-resolve to a hosting provider. What is the right interpretation?
options: It indicates a crawl budget increase
Google is using a new data centre
It is likely a spoofed bot and should be excluded from Googlebot analysis
pool.explanation: Genuine Googlebot IPs resolve to Google domains or match Google's published ranges; others are impostors.

pool.question: Which status code is best for content permanently moved to a new URL?
pool.explanation: 301 (or 308) signals a permanent move and is a strong canonical signal for the target.

pool.question: An audit finds `/a → /b → /c → /d` redirect chains on 4,000 URLs. What is the correct remediation? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Point each legacy URL directly to the final destination
Update internal links to the final URLs
Leave them because Google follows up to 10 hops
pool.explanation: Flatten to one hop and remove internal links to redirects. Google following hops does not make chains free; 302s weaken the signal.

pool.question: Page A declares rel=canonical to page B, but B returns a 301 to C. What is the issue?
options: The canonical target is not an indexable 200 URL, sending conflicting signals
pool.explanation: Canonical targets should be final, indexable 200 URLs; canonical-to-redirect weakens and confuses the signal.

pool.question: Which is the recommended canonical on page 4 of a paginated blog archive?
pool.explanation: Paginated pages are distinct and should self-canonicalise.

pool.question: A marketplace wants brand + category facet pages indexed but sort, price and multi-select combinations kept out of crawling. Which plan fits Google's faceted navigation guidance?
options: Canonicalise all facets to the category and allow crawling
noindex every facet including brand pages
Static clean URLs for demand-backed facets; robots.txt disallow for sort/price/multi-select parameters; 404 for empty combinations
pool.explanation: Index only facets with demand using clean URLs, block low-value parameter spaces from crawling, and return 404 on empty results.

pool.question: A retailer 301-redirects 8,000 discontinued, unrelated product URLs to the home page. How will Google likely treat these?
options: As strong relevance signals for the home page
pool.explanation: Irrelevant mass redirects to the home page are commonly treated as soft 404s; use relevant targets or 404/410.

pool.question: Which statement about duplicate content on your own site is accurate?
options: It mainly splits signals and lets Google choose a canonical you may not want
pool.explanation: Ordinary duplication is not penalised; the cost is signal splitting, crawl waste and unpredictable canonical selection.

pool.question: What is an orphan page?
options: A page with no outbound links
A page that exists but has no internal links pointing to it
pool.explanation: Orphans are not reachable by following internal links, so discovery depends on sitemaps or external links.

pool.question: How many URLs can a single XML sitemap file contain?
pool.explanation: Up to 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed per file; use a sitemap index for more.

pool.question: A plugin sets every URL's lastmod to the sitemap generation time daily. Consequence?
options: Google may learn lastmod is unreliable and ignore it
pool.explanation: Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently accurate; fake freshness teaches it to ignore the field.

pool.question: Which XML sitemap practices are correct? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Split sitemaps by template to diagnose indexing by section
Reference the sitemap index in robots.txt
Set priority to 1.0 on money pages to rank them higher
pool.explanation: Clean URLs, segmentation and robots.txt references are best practice. Google ignores priority.

pool.question: A high-revenue guide sits at click depth 8 with two internal links from paginated archives. Which intervention is most likely to improve its crawl frequency and internal signals?
options: Add nofollow to other blog links
Add it to the sitemap with changefreq=daily
Link it from a relevant hub in main navigation and from related service pages with descriptive anchors
pool.explanation: Contextual internal links from prominent, relevant pages reduce depth and pass signals; changefreq is ignored and internal nofollow does not reallocate value.

pool.question: Why add BreadcrumbList structured data alongside visible breadcrumbs?
options: It helps Google understand hierarchy and can make the page eligible for breadcrumb display in results
pool.explanation: Breadcrumb markup aids understanding and presentation; it is not a ranking guarantee or an indexing requirement.

pool.question: What does the x-default hreflang value indicate?
options: The fallback page for users whose language/region is not matched
pool.explanation: x-default designates the default or selector page for unmatched users.

pool.question: The /ar-sa/ pages canonicalise to /en/ equivalents while hreflang lists both. Result?
options: Google may drop /ar-sa/ from the cluster because the pages declare themselves non-canonical
Nothing; canonicals are ignored on international sites
pool.explanation: hreflang should reference canonical URLs; each language version must self-canonicalise.

pool.question: Which hreflang implementations are valid? (Choose all that apply.)
pool.explanation: ar-ae (Arabic, UAE) and ur-pk (Urdu, Pakistan) are valid. en-uk uses an invalid region code (GB is correct) and a region alone is invalid.

pool.question: Which format does Google recommend for structured data?
pool.explanation: Google supports several formats but recommends JSON-LD for ease of implementation and maintenance.

pool.question: After adding valid Product markup, rich results do not appear. What is the most accurate explanation?
options: Valid markup makes a page eligible, but Google decides whether to show rich results
Google needs a Merchant Center account for any rich result
Rich results only show after 12 months
pool.explanation: Eligibility is not a guarantee; quality, relevance and other factors influence display.

pool.question: Which is a structured data policy violation?
options: Marking up the price visible on the page
Adding AggregateRating markup for reviews that are not shown on the page
Including sameAs links to official profiles
pool.explanation: Markup must reflect visible content. Invisible or fabricated reviews are misleading and can cause a manual action.

pool.question: What is the 'good' threshold for INP?
pool.explanation: INP is good at 200 ms or less at the 75th percentile.

pool.question: Mobile CLS is poor on article pages. Ads load into slots with no reserved height. Which fix addresses the cause?
options: Reserve space for ad slots with min-height or aspect-ratio
pool.explanation: Unreserved ad slots push content down; reserving space prevents layout shifts.

pool.question: INP field data is poor on a product page. A trace shows a 450 ms task running on click of 'Add to basket' from a third-party personalisation script. Which actions are appropriate? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Break up the long task and yield to the main thread
Give immediate visual feedback and defer the non-essential work
Review whether the third-party script is needed or can load later
pool.explanation: INP is about main-thread work after interactions. Feedback, yielding and trimming third-party JS address it; LCP preload does not.

pool.question: Which statement about mobile-first indexing is correct?
options: Desktop content is used if mobile lacks it
Tabs and accordions are never indexed
Content removed from the mobile HTML is effectively invisible to Google
pool.explanation: Google indexes the mobile version. Content in collapsed UI in the HTML is fine; content absent from mobile HTML is lost.

pool.question: Which data source reflects real-user Core Web Vitals?
pool.explanation: CrUX field data, surfaced in PageSpeed Insights and Search Console, reflects real users.

pool.question: Before enabling HSTS with includeSubDomains, what must you confirm?
options: That every subdomain serves valid HTTPS
pool.explanation: includeSubDomains forces HTTPS on all subdomains; any HTTP-only subdomain becomes unreachable for returning browsers.

pool.question: What should happen first when planning a site migration?
options: Benchmark crawl, Search Console, analytics, rankings and backlinks
Change the domain in Search Console
pool.explanation: Benchmarks let you verify parity and diagnose any post-launch drop.

pool.question: After launch, traffic collapses. The new site's robots.txt contains `Disallow: /` copied from staging. Which steps are right? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Wait a month before changing anything
Check the robots.txt report in Search Console to confirm Google refetched the new file
Add rollback and robots.txt checks to the release checklist
pool.explanation: Fix fast, confirm Google has the new file, and prevent recurrence. Waiting prolongs the damage.

pool.question: Which is the correct redirect mapping principle for a replatform?
options: Each old URL to its most relevant new equivalent in one hop; intentional 404/410 where none exists
Only redirect URLs that are in the old sitemap
All old URLs to the home page
pool.explanation: Relevant one-hop 301s preserve signals; honest 404/410 for no-equivalent pages avoids soft 404s.

pool.question: A migration went live six weeks ago. Old URLs 301 correctly, but many new URLs show 'Discovered – currently not indexed' and logs show few Googlebot hits to them. What is the most useful next step?
options: Check crawl capacity (server response time, 5xx) and internal linking/sitemaps to new URLs, and review Crawl stats
pool.explanation: Discovered-not-crawled suggests capacity or demand issues; investigate server health, crawl stats and discovery paths.

pool.question: Which Search Console report shows the Google-selected canonical for a single URL?
pool.explanation: URL Inspection shows user-declared and Google-selected canonicals.

pool.question: Why can the query table in Search Console show fewer clicks than the page table for the same period?
options: Only desktop is shown by query
Clicks from anonymised queries are omitted from query-level data
Bots are included in page data
pool.explanation: Rare queries are anonymised and omitted from query rows, so totals differ.
